content: The initial tracking information for the Early ACS study was first received on August 17, 2004, and the last update was made on December 17, 2008. The study officially began in November 2004. The primary outcome measures, submitted on January 3, 2008, include the incidence of a composite outcome consisting of death, myocardial infarction (MI), recurrent ischemia requiring urgent revascularization (RI-UR), and thrombotic bailout. The secondary outcome measures, also submitted on January 3, 2008, focus on key metrics such as the incidence of death/MI, the incidence of MI alone, the composite incidence of death/MI/RI-UR, and the incidence of death alone. The study, titled EARLY ACS: Early Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa Inhibition in Patients With Non-ST-Segment Elevation Acute Coronary Syndrome, was a randomized, placebo-controlled trial. Its purpose was to evaluate the clinical benefits of early, front-loaded eptifibatide (INTEGRILIN®) therapy in patients with non-ST-segment elevation acute coronary syndrome (NSTE-ACS). The study aimed to determine whether early administration of eptifibatide could reduce the occurrence of death, heart attack, and urgent cardiac interventions (such as surgery) compared to placebo. Patients enrolled in the study experienced symptoms of acute coronary syndrome, such as chest pain at rest lasting at least 10 minutes, and were planned to undergo invasive surgical procedures after receiving the study drug for 12 to 96 hours. The study included two treatment groups: one receiving eptifibatide in addition to standard care and the other receiving a placebo alongside standard care. The likelihood of being assigned to either group was 50/50, akin to a coin toss. All patients received standard-of-care medications, including aspirin and either unfractionated heparin (UFH) or low-molecular-weight heparin, as determined by the investigator. This was a Phase III interventional study with a randomized, double-blind design (blinding the subject, investigator, and outcomes assessor) and parallel assignment. The study assessed both safety and efficacy. The condition under investigation was myocardial ischemia in the context of acute coronary syndrome. The interventions included the drug eptifibatide (INTEGRILIN®) and a placebo. The study arms consisted of an experimental group receiving eptifibatide in addition to standard care and a placebo comparator group receiving placebo alongside standard care. The recruitment status of the study was Completed, with an estimated enrollment and completion date in November 2008. The primary completion date, which marked the final data collection for the primary outcome measure, was also November 2008. Eligibility criteria for inclusion required participants to be willing and able to provide informed consent, comply with study procedures, and complete follow-up for one year. Participants needed to be randomized within 12 hours of experiencing acute coronary syndrome symptoms and planned to undergo an invasive strategy after receiving the study drug for 12 to 96 hours. Inclusion criteria also required patients to have symptoms of cardiac ischemia at rest (angina or anginal equivalent) lasting at least 10 minutes and meeting at least two of the following criteria: age 60 years or older, electrocardiogram (ECG) changes, or elevated troponin or CK-MB levels. Alternatively, patients could qualify if they met all three of the following criteria: prior history of cardiovascular disease, elevated troponin or CK-MB levels, and age 50-59 years. Exclusion criteria included known or suspected pregnancy, recent renal dialysis (within 30 days), serious illnesses or conditions deemed hazardous by the investigator, history of hemorrhagic stroke or recent non-hemorrhagic stroke (within 7 days), central nervous system damage (e.g., neoplasm, aneurysm, intracranial surgery), bleeding disorders (including gastrointestinal bleeding), recent major surgery or trauma, certain hematologic problems following treatment with heparin or eptifibatide, and recent therapy with related drugs. The study accepted both male and female participants aged 18 years and older but did not accept healthy volunteers. The study was sponsored by Schering-Plough, with Duke University listed as a collaborator. The responsible party for the study was the Head of the Clinical Trials Registry & Results Disclosure Group at Schering-Plough. The study was registered under the identifier NCT00089895, and the verification date was December 2008.
